name: Braces / orthodontics for jaw shape

lead: Braces and other orthodontic appliances move teeth and, in growing patients, guide jaws. People interested in appearance discuss them for bite and profile.
Severe jaw discrepancies may need surgery combined with orthodontics.

paras: Appliances apply sustained force to move teeth through bone; palatal expanders and headgear act on jaw alignment [1].
Decalcification and decay with poor hygiene, and frequent relapse, are described; retainers are often recommended [1].

lead: Orthodontics is the dental specialty that diagnoses and corrects misaligned teeth, jaws and bite patterns, and can modify facial growth; braces are its best-known tool [1]. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to improve bite and facial profile, often alongside jaw surgery.

Wikipedia notes that clinicians learned that perfect occlusion alone does not ensure good facial appearance, and that headgear and palatal expansion can alter jaw alignment or airflow [1]. Severe malocclusions may need jaw surgery followed by orthodontics [1].
Registered trials in the area mostly address alignment speed, sleep and airway, rather than facial attractiveness.
infobox: Over 50% show some relapse within 10 years (retainers advised)

paras: Treatment typically starts before adulthood, when bone is more adjustable, and uses braces and other appliances [1]. Abnormal tooth and jaw alignment is common, with worldwide prevalence reported as high as 56% [1].

Attempts to straighten teeth date to about 1000 BC; modern orthodontics developed in the mid-1800s with figures such as Norman Kingsley and Edward Angle. Cephalometric X-rays after World War II showed many Class II and III problems arise from jaw relationships [1]. Bonded brackets replaced wrapped bands by the mid-1970s [1].
Fixed appliances are not preferred in patients with poor oral hygiene because of decalcification and decay, and relapse is common [1].

Registered studies include a trial on speeding alignment of crowded lower front teeth (n=38) [2], research on speech in patients with dentofacial deformities before and after treatment (n=180, recruiting) [3], and trials of functional orthodontic appliances and sleep or airway outcomes in children [4][5]. A trial of maxillary expansion in paediatric sleep apnoea enrolled 14 participants [6]. Wikipedia notes that conclusive scientific evidence for health benefits is lacking, though treated patients report higher quality of life [1].

timeline.event: Greek and Etruscan evidence of attempts to treat crooked teeth [1].
Lawrence Andrews defines ideal occlusion; straight-wire appliance follows around 1976 [1].
